questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.sub_topic: Sultan when Ibn Battuta reached Delhi
questions.question: Ibn Battuta reached Delhi in 1333, and the Sultan, impressed by his scholarship, appointed him the qazi or judge of Delhi. That Sultan was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Muhammad bin Tughlaq
Why: Ibn Battuta served Muhammad bin Tughlaq as qazi of Delhi. He later fell out of favour and was sent to China as the Sultan's envoy.
Why not the others: (B) Alauddin Khalji and (C) Iltutmish ruled before 1333. (D) Firuz Shah Tughlaq succeeded Muhammad bin Tughlaq in 1351.
Key point: Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier, Morocco, and travelled widely before reaching India.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.sub_topic: Period of composition of the Mahabharata
questions.question: NCERT notes that the Mahabharata, as we have it today, was composed over a period of about ____, beginning around 500 BCE.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1,000 years
Why: The text was composed over about 1,000 years from c. 500 BCE, and some stories may be even older. That is why it reflects many changing social situations.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are far too short for a text with so many layers. (D) would take it back long before the period NCERT discusses.
Key point: The critical edition, prepared under V.S. Sukthankar, compared Sanskrit manuscripts from across the subcontinent.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question:
Arrange the following travellers in the order in which they came to the subcontinent, earliest first:
(A) François Bernier
(B) Abdur Razzaq Samarqandi
(C) Al-Biruni
(D) Ibn Battuta
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (C), (D), (B), (A)
Why: Al-Biruni came in the eleventh century, after Sultan Mahmud's conquest of Khwarizm. Ibn Battuta reached Delhi in 1333. Abdur Razzaq came in the 1440s. Bernier was in India from 1656 to 1668.
Why not the others: (A) puts Abdur Razzaq before Ibn Battuta. (C) puts Ibn Battuta before al-Biruni. (D) puts Bernier before Abdur Razzaq.
Key point: The three main travellers in NCERT fall in different centuries: eleventh, fourteenth and seventeenth.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question: The Congress session held at Lahore in December 1929, which adopted complete independence (Purna Swaraj) as its goal, was presided over by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Jawaharlal Nehru
Why: Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the Lahore session. NCERT notes this as the young Nehru's "baptism by fire" into the leadership of the Congress.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) did not preside over this session.
Key point: After the Lahore session, 26 January 1930 was observed as "Independence Day" across the country.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.question: The discussions of the Constituent Assembly took place between December 1946 and November 1949. They were held in:
options: A) 6 sessions with sittings over 100 days
B) 8 sessions with sittings over 120 days
C) 12 sessions with sittings over 200 days
D) 11 sessions with sittings over 165 days
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 11 sessions with sittings over 165 days
Why: The Assembly held eleven sessions, with sittings spread over 165 days. Between sessions, committees and sub-committees revised the drafts.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) give the wrong numbers.
Key point: The Constitution was signed in November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question: The Greek ambassador whose account, known as the *Indica*, is one of the major sources for the Mauryan empire was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Megasthenes
Why: Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador at the court of Chandragupta Maurya. His *Indica* survives in fragments quoted by later Greek and Roman writers.
Why not the others: (B) Ptolemy was a geographer. (C) Herodotus wrote about the Persian wars. (D) Thucydides wrote a history of the Peloponnesian War. None of them was an ambassador at the Mauryan court.
Key point: Mauryan sources include Megasthenes, the *Arthashastra*, later Buddhist, Jaina and Puranic texts, and Ashoka's inscriptions.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Permanent Settlement in Bengal:
(A) It was introduced in 1793, when Charles Cornwallis was Governor-General.
(B) The revenue that each zamindar had to pay was fixed permanently.
(C) The "Sunset Law" allowed a zamindar to delay payment until sunset on the last day of the following year.
(D) Jotedars were rich peasants who controlled large areas of land in the villages.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) follow NCERT. The settlement came in 1793 under Cornwallis, the revenue was fixed in perpetuity, and the jotedars were rich peasants who grew powerful at the zamindars' expense.
Why not the others: (C) is false. Under the Sunset Law, if payment did not come in by sunset on the specified date, the zamindari was liable to be auctioned. Options (A), (B) and (D) all include (C).
Key point: Many zamindaris were auctioned after 1793, because the revenue demand was high and had to be paid on time.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question: On 10 May 1857, sepoys broke into the bell of arms, attacked white officers and freed comrades who had been imprisoned for refusing the new cartridges. This took place at the cantonment in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Meerut
Why: The mutiny began at Meerut on the afternoon of 10 May 1857. The sepoys then rode to Delhi and asked Bahadur Shah Zafar to lead the revolt.
Why not the others: (A) Delhi was where the sepoys went next. (B) Lucknow saw the siege of the Residency. (C) Kanpur rose under Nana Sahib.
Key point: The bell of arms was the storeroom where arms and ammunition were kept.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question: The idea that grew in Mahayana Buddhism of compassionate beings who gather merit through their efforts and use it to help others, rather than attaining nibbana and leaving the world, refers to:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Bodhisattas
Why: In the Mahayana, Bodhisattas were seen as perfectly compassionate beings who used their merit to help others. Their worship became a central part of the tradition.
Why not the others: (B) Arhats sought their own liberation, the older (Hinayana or Theravada) ideal. (C) Tirthankaras belong to Jainism. (D) Bhikkhunis were women who joined the sangha.
Key point: The Mahayana ("great vehicle") also began to show the Buddha in images, not only through symbols.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Text)
(A) Vinaya Pitaka
(B) Sutta Pitaka
(C) Abhidhamma Pitaka
(D) Therigatha

List-II (Content)
(I) Philosophical matters
(II) Rules for those who joined the sangha
(III) Verses composed by bhikkhunis
(IV) The teachings of the Buddha
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: The Vinaya Pitaka has the rules for the sangha (II), the Sutta Pitaka the Buddha's teachings (IV) and the Abhidhamma Pitaka philosophical matters (I). The Therigatha, part of the Sutta Pitaka, is a collection of verses by bhikkhunis (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the Vinaya and the Sutta. (C) swaps the Sutta and the Abhidhamma. (D) swaps the Abhidhamma and the Therigatha.
Key point: Tipitaka means "three baskets", the baskets in which the texts were first stored.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Leader)
(A) Shah Mal
(B) Gonoo
(C) Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah
(D) Kunwar Singh

List-II (Region)
(I) Singhbhum in Chotanagpur
(II) Pargana Barout in Uttar Pradesh
(III) Arrah in Bihar
(IV) Faizabad in Awadh
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: Shah Mal mobilised the villages of pargana Barout (II). Gonoo, a tribal cultivator, led the Kols of Singhbhum (I). Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah, who had been preaching jihad, was based at Faizabad (IV). Kunwar Singh was a zamindar of Arrah (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Gonoo and the maulvi. (B) swaps Shah Mal and Gonoo. (D) swaps the maulvi and Kunwar Singh.
Key point: The revolt threw up local leaders: peasants, tribals, religious figures and zamindars.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.question: In the Jaina tradition, Mahavira is regarded as the twenty-fourth tirthankara. The word tirthankara refers to:
options: A) Monks who lived in caves cut into hills
B) Those who guide people across the river of existence
C) Kings who protected Jaina monasteries
D) Teachers who compiled the Jaina texts in Sanskrit
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Those who guide people across the river of existence
Why: Tirthankaras are "those who guide men and women across the river of existence". Mahavira was preceded by 23 tirthankaras.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) describe other people. None of them gives the meaning of the term.
Key point: The basic Jaina idea is that the entire world is animated, and that is the basis of its emphasis on ahimsa.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.sub_topic: Roles in the making of the Constitution
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Person)
(A) Rajendra Prasad
(B) B.R. Ambedkar
(C) Jawaharlal Nehru
(D) S.N. Mukherjee

List-II (Role)
(I) Chief draughtsman, who put complex proposals into clear legal language
(II) Moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946
(III) President of the Constituent Assembly
(IV) Chairman of the Drafting Committee
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Rajendra Prasad was President of the Assembly (III). Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee (IV). Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution (II). S.N. Mukherjee was the chief draughtsman (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Prasad and Ambedkar. (C) swaps Ambedkar and Nehru. (D) swaps Nehru and Mukherjee.
Key point: Ambedkar was given the task of piloting the Draft Constitution through the Assembly.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question: After the failure of the Cripps Mission, Gandhi launched the Quit India Movement in ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) August 1942
Why: Gandhi launched Quit India in August 1942. He and other leaders were jailed at once, but the movement continued through young activists.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not the dates of the launch. 1945 is the year Gandhi and other leaders were released and talks began.
Key point: Quit India was a genuine mass movement, bringing into its ambit hundreds of thousands of ordinary Indians.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question: The Virashaiva (Lingayat) tradition of Karnataka, which challenged caste and questioned rituals, grew out of a movement led in the twelfth century by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Basavanna
Why: Basavanna, a brahmana who was a minister at the Kalachuri court, led the movement from which the Virashaivas or Lingayats grew.
Why not the others: (A) Appar and (D) Sambandar were Nayanars of Tamil Nadu. (B) Chaitanya was a Vaishnava saint of Bengal.
Key point: Lingayats worship Shiva as a linga and question the theory of rebirth and the idea of pollution.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.question: The Fifth Report, which ran to over 1,000 pages and became the basis of intense debate in England about the East India Company's rule, was submitted to the British Parliament in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1813
Why: The Fifth Report was submitted to the British Parliament in 1813. It was the fifth of a series of reports on the administration of the East India Company.
Why not the others: (A) 1793 is the year of the Permanent Settlement. (B) 1800 is when Mackenzie mapped Hampi. (C) 1857 is the year of the revolt.
Key point: The Report reproduced petitions of zamindars and ryots in its appendices, but it should be read critically, as an official text.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question: In 1565 the Vijayanagara army was defeated at the battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi (Talikota) by the combined forces of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda. The army was led by its chief minister:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Rama Raya
Why: Rama Raya, the chief minister, led the Vijayanagara army at Rakshasi-Tangadi in 1565. The victors then sacked the city, which was abandoned within a few years.
Why not the others: (A) Krishnadeva Raya died in 1529. (C) Harihara was one of the founders of the empire in 1336. (D) Achyuta Deva Raya ruled in the 1530s.
Key point: The city's destruction in 1565 marks the end of Vijayanagara as an imperial capital.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.sub_topic: Barriers to understanding noted by al-Biruni
questions.question: Al-Biruni identified several "barriers" that he felt stood in the way of understanding India. Which of the following was NOT one of them?
options: A) Differences in language, as Sanskrit was very different from Arabic and Persian
B) Differences in religious beliefs and practices
C) The self-absorption and insularity of the local population
D) The absence of any written texts in India to learn from
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The absence of any written texts in India to learn from
Why: Al-Biruni relied heavily on Sanskrit works such as the Vedas, the Puranas, the *Bhagavad Gita* and the Manusmriti. He could not have called the absence of texts a barrier.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are the three barriers he named: language, religious difference, and the insularity of local people.
Key point: Despite these barriers, al-Biruni based his account almost entirely on Brahmanical Sanskrit texts.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question: The system of "subsidiary alliance", under which a ruler had to keep British forces in his territory and could not have his own armed forces, was devised in 1798 by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Lord Wellesley
Why: Lord Wellesley devised the subsidiary alliance in 1798. Awadh was made to accept it in 1801.
Why not the others: (B) Dalhousie annexed Awadh in 1856. (C) Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in 1793. (D) Canning was Governor-General during the revolt of 1857.
Key point: The subsidiary alliance left rulers dependent on the British, who then annexed states on grounds such as "misgovernment".

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question: In the Sufi tradition, the term khanqah refers to:
options: A) The tomb of a Sufi saint, which became a place of pilgrimage
B) A hospice where the shaikh lived and met disciples and visitors
C) The ritual of music and dance used to evoke mystical ecstasy
D) A chain of transmission linking a master to the Prophet
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A hospice where the shaikh lived and met disciples and visitors
Why: The khanqah was the hospice, the centre of a Sufi community, where the master (shaikh, pir) lived and received disciples (murids) and visitors.
Why not the others: (A) is a dargah. (C) is sama'. (D) is a silsila.
Key point: Visiting a saint's tomb is ziyarat, and the saint's death anniversary is the urs.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Inscription)
(A) Prayaga prashasti
(B) Junagadh rock inscription
(C) Copper-plate grant of Prabhavati Gupta
(D) Rock and pillar edicts of Ashoka

List-II (What it records)
(I) A grant of land to a brahmana in a village, issued by a Vakataka queen
(II) The ruler's message of dhamma, mostly in Prakrit and in the Brahmi script
(III) The repair of the Sudarshana lake by the Shaka ruler Rudradaman
(IV) Praise of Samudragupta, composed by his court poet Harisena
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: The Prayaga prashasti (Allahabad pillar) praises Samudragupta and was composed by Harisena (IV). The Junagadh inscription records Rudradaman's repair of the Sudarshana lake (III). Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II and a Vakataka queen, granted land in Danguna village (I). Ashoka's edicts carry his message of dhamma, mostly in Prakrit and in the Brahmi script (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the Junagadh inscription and the land grant. (C) swaps the two prashasti-type records in (A) and (B). (D) swaps the land grant and the edicts.
Key point: Prashastis praise a ruler and need to be read critically. Land grants show how rulers gave land to religious groups.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.sub_topic: Rules about marriage in Brahmanical texts
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about marriage and property in the Brahmanical texts:
(A) The Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras recognised eight forms of marriage.
(B) Of these forms, the first four were considered "good", while the rest were condemned.
(C) Kanyadana, the gift of a daughter in marriage, was described as an important religious duty of the father.
(D) The Manusmriti gave daughters an equal share with sons in the paternal estate.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) follow NCERT. The texts recognised eight forms of marriage, the first four were "good", and kanyadana was the father's religious duty.
Why not the others: (D) is false. According to the Manusmriti the paternal estate was divided equally among the sons, with a special share for the eldest. Women could keep stridhana, the gifts received at marriage. Options (B), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: The condemned forms of marriage may have been practised by those who did not accept Brahmanical norms.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.sub_topic: The village panchayat in Mughal India
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the village panchayat in Mughal India:
(A) Membership was open to every villager, including landless labourers, on equal terms.
(B) The headman (muqaddam or mandal) was chosen through the consensus of the village elders and approved by the zamindar.
(C) The panchayat could impose fines and even expel a member from the community.
(D) The panchayat had its own common fund, to which all villagers contributed.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why: (B), (C) and (D) follow NCERT. The muqaddam was chosen by consensus and approved by the zamindar. The panchayat could fine or expel people, and its common fund paid for village expenses and even for relief during natural calamities.
Why not the others: (A) is false. The panchayat was an assembly of elders, usually important people with hereditary rights in their property, and in mixed-caste villages it was usually a heterogeneous body. Options (A) and (B) include (A), and option (C) leaves out the true statement (D).
Key point: Expulsion was a strong deterrent, because the person was forced to leave the village and became an outcaste.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.sub_topic: Year of Gandhi's return to India
questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi returned to India after two decades in South Africa, where he had first forged the techniques of satyagraha, in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) January 1915
Why: Gandhi returned to India in January 1915.
Why not the others: (A) 1909 is the year of *Hind Swaraj*. (B) 1919 is the year of the Rowlatt Act. (C) 1912 has no significance in his return.
Key point: His first major public appearance in India was at the opening of Banaras Hindu University in February 1916.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Alvars and Nayanars of Tamil Nadu:
(A) Tradition counts twelve Alvars, devotees of Vishnu, and sixty-three Nayanars, devotees of Shiva.
(B) The Nalayira Divyaprabandham is a compilation of the compositions of the Nayanars.
(C) Karaikkal Ammaiyar, a woman devotee of Shiva, is counted among the Nayanars.
(D) The Tevaram is a collection of the compositions of Nayanar saints.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: (A), (C) and (D) follow NCERT. There were 12 Alvars and 63 Nayanars. Karaikkal Ammaiyar was a Nayanar, and the Tevaram collects the Nayanars' poems.
Why not the others: (B) is false. The Nalayira Divyaprabandham ("four thousand sacred compositions") is the anthology of the Alvars' compositions. Options (A), (C) and (D) all include (B).
Key point: Andal was a woman Alvar. Karaikkal Ammaiyar was a woman Nayanar.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question: In the Mahabharata, Bhima married the rakshasa woman Hidimba. Their son, who later fought on the side of the Pandavas, was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Ghatotkacha
Why: Ghatotkacha was the son of Bhima and Hidimba. He joined the Pandavas in the war against the Kauravas.
Why not the others: (A) Abhimanyu was the son of Arjuna. (B) Ashvatthama was the son of Drona and fought for the Kauravas. (C) Ekalavya was a forest-dwelling nishada who learnt archery by himself.
Key point: Historians read the Hidimba story as a sign of contact between the Pandavas and forest-dwelling peoples.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) The Lahore session of the Congress adopts the goal of Purna Swaraj
(B) The Gandhi–Irwin Pact
(C) The Champaran campaign for indigo cultivators
(D) The countrywide campaign against the Rowlatt Act
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: Champaran came in 1917, the campaign against the Rowlatt Act in 1919, the Lahore session's Purna Swaraj resolution in December 1929, and the Gandhi–Irwin Pact in March 1931.
Why not the others: (A) puts Lahore before the Rowlatt campaign. (B) puts the Rowlatt campaign before Champaran. (D) puts the Pact before the Lahore session.
Key point: The Gandhi–Irwin Pact ended Civil Disobedience and led to Gandhi attending the second Round Table Conference.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Religious History: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions
questions.question: The verses attributed to Kabir have come down in three distinct traditions. The collection preserved by the Kabirpanth in Varanasi and elsewhere in Uttar Pradesh is the ____.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Bijak
Why: The *Bijak* is preserved by the Kabirpanth (the sect of Kabir) in Varanasi and elsewhere in Uttar Pradesh.
Why not the others: (B) The *Kabir Granthavali* is associated with the Dadupanth in Rajasthan. (A) The *Adi Granth Sahib* also contains many of Kabir's compositions, but it is the Sikh scripture. (C) The Tevaram is a Tamil Shaiva collection.
Key point: Kabir described the Ultimate Reality in many ways, as Allah, Hari, Ram and Alakh.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Person)
(A) Colin Mackenzie
(B) Krishnadeva Raya
(C) Domingo Paes
(D) Abdur Razzaq

List-II (Connection with Vijayanagara)
(I) Engineer and surveyor who prepared the first survey map of Hampi
(II) Ambassador sent by the ruler of Persia, who described the city's fortifications
(III) Ruler who wrote the *Amuktamalyada*, a Telugu work on statecraft
(IV) Portuguese visitor who described the city and the king's palace
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Colin Mackenzie, later the first Surveyor General of India, prepared the first survey map of Hampi (I). Krishnadeva Raya wrote the *Amuktamalyada* (III). Domingo Paes was a Portuguese visitor (IV). Abdur Razzaq, ambassador from Persia, admired the seven lines of fortification (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Mackenzie and Krishnadeva Raya. (B) swaps the two foreign visitors. (C) swaps the Portuguese visitor and the king.
Key point: Hampi's ruins were brought to light in 1800 by Colin Mackenzie.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.question: Francis Buchanan described the Paharias, who lived by shifting cultivation, hunting and collecting forest produce. They lived around:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The Rajmahal hills
Why: The Paharias lived around the Rajmahal hills in what is now Jharkhand.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are hill ranges in other parts of India. None of them is linked with the Paharias in NCERT.
Key point: When the Santhals settled in the lower slopes, the Paharias were pushed deeper into the hills.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question: The name Hampi, by which the ruins of Vijayanagara are known, is derived from the name of:
options: A) Pampadevi, a local mother goddess
B) Harihara, a founder of the empire
C) A river that flows south of the city
D) A Portuguese visitor to the city
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Pampadevi, a local mother goddess
Why: Hampi takes its name from Pampadevi, the local mother goddess.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) have no connection with the name. The river at Hampi is the Tungabhadra.
Key point: The Virupaksha temple at Hampi was the guardian deity's temple of the Vijayanagara kings.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Colonialism and Rural Society: Evidence from Official Reports
questions.sub_topic: Chronology of events in rural colonial India
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) The revolt of the Santhals against colonial rule
(B) The submission of the Fifth Report to Parliament
(C) The Deccan riots against moneylenders
(D) The introduction of the Permanent Settlement in Bengal
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (D), (B), (A), (C)
Why: The Permanent Settlement came in 1793 and the Fifth Report in 1813. The Santhals revolted in 1855–56, and the Deccan riots broke out in 1875.
Why not the others: (B) puts the Santhal revolt before the Fifth Report. (C) puts the Fifth Report before the Permanent Settlement. (D) puts the Deccan riots before the Santhal revolt.
Key point: Each event left behind an official record: the Fifth Report, Buchanan's reports, and the Deccan Riots Commission report.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question:
Arrange the following rulers in chronological order, earliest first:
(A) Samudragupta
(B) Kanishka
(C) Chandragupta Maurya
(D) Ashoka
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C), (D), (B), (A)
Why: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan empire c. 321 BCE. His grandson Ashoka ruled in the third century BCE. Kanishka, the best-known Kushana ruler, belongs to the first or second century CE. Samudragupta, the Gupta ruler, belongs to the fourth century CE.
Why not the others: (A) puts Kanishka before Ashoka. (B) puts Ashoka before his grandfather Chandragupta. (C) puts the Gupta ruler before the Kushana ruler.
Key point: Mauryas (c. 321–187 BCE) → Kushanas (c. first century BCE–first century CE onwards) → Guptas (from the fourth century CE).

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.sub_topic: Gandhi's view on a national language
questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi felt that everyone should speak a language that common people could easily understand, a blend of Hindi and Urdu. He called this language:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Hindustani
Why: Gandhi favoured Hindustani, a mix of Hindi and Urdu spoken by a large section of people, as the national language.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) are the narrower forms he thought would divide people. (D) English was the language he wanted Indians to move away from.
Key point: The Assembly finally made Hindi in the Devanagari script the official language, with English continuing for fifteen years.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: The Making of the Constitution
questions.sub_topic: Composition and working of the Assembly
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Constituent Assembly:
(A) Its members were elected by the provincial legislatures, not by universal adult franchise.
(B) The Muslim League chose to boycott its early sessions.
(C) The Constitution it drafted came into effect on 26 November 1949.
(D) It completed the Constitution within six months of its first meeting.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A) and (B) only
Why: (A) and (B) follow NCERT. Members were elected by the provincial legislatures formed under the 1946 elections, and the Muslim League boycotted the early sessions.
Why not the others: (C) is false, because the Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950. (D) is false, because the work took almost three years, from December 1946 to November 1949. Options (A), (B) and (D) each include a false statement.
Key point: The Congress dominated the Assembly, holding 82% of its seats after the Muslim League's boycott.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.question: The *Ain-i Akbari*, the most important source for the agrarian history of the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, was written by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Abu'l Fazl
Why: Abu'l Fazl, a court historian of Akbar, wrote the *Ain-i Akbari*, completed in 1598 after five revisions.
Why not the others: (A) Badauni wrote a critical history of Akbar's reign. (B) Lahori wrote the *Badshah Nama* for Shah Jahan. (D) Muhammad Kazim wrote the *Alamgir Nama* for Aurangzeb.
Key point: The *Ain* records the state's arrangements for agriculture, revenue and administration. Its picture is drawn from the centre's point of view.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Mahatma Gandhi and National Movements
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Non-Cooperation Movement:
(A) Gandhi hoped that by coupling Non-Cooperation with the Khilafat Movement, Hindus and Muslims could together end colonial rule.
(B) After a crowd set fire to a police station at Chauri Chaura in February 1922, Gandhi called off the movement.
(C) Students stopped going to government-run schools, and lawyers refused to attend court.
(D) The working class did not take part, because Gandhi asked factory workers to stay out of the movement.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) follow NCERT. Non-Cooperation was joined with Khilafat, it was withdrawn after Chauri Chaura, and students and lawyers boycotted government institutions.
Why not the others: (D) is false. NCERT notes that the working class went on strike in many towns and cities. Options (B), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Non-Cooperation shook British rule more than anything since 1857.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Vijayanagara Empire: Politics, Economy and Architecture
questions.question: Identify the incorrectly matched pair of a Vijayanagara dynasty and the information given about it:
options: A) Sangama – founded by Harihara and Bukka in 1336
B) Tuluva – the dynasty of Krishnadeva Raya
C) Aravidu – founded the empire in 1336
D) Saluva – military commanders who seized power in 1485
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Aravidu – founded the empire in 1336
Why: The Aravidu dynasty was the last of the four. It came to power in 1570, after the defeat at Talikota, and it did not found the empire.
Why not the others: (A) The Sangamas founded the empire in 1336. (B) Krishnadeva Raya belonged to the Tuluva dynasty. (D) The Saluvas, who were military commanders, seized power in 1485.
Key point: Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.question: Tobacco reached the Deccan and then north India in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Which Mughal emperor tried to ban smoking it, though the ban had no effect?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Jahangir
Why: Jahangir was concerned about the spread of tobacco smoking and imposed a ban. It had no effect: by the end of the seventeenth century tobacco was one of the main items of cultivation and trade.
Why not the others: (A) Akbar and his nobles first came across tobacco in 1604, but he did not ban it. (C) and (D) are not linked with this ban.
Key point: New crops from the New World, such as tobacco, maize, chillies and potatoes, came into India in this period.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: History of Buddhism and Jainism: Cultural Developments
questions.sub_topic: Incorrectly matched stupa and present-day state
questions.question: Identify the incorrectly matched pair of an early stupa and the present-day state in which it stands:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Amaravati – Tamil Nadu
Why: Amaravati is in Andhra Pradesh, not Tamil Nadu. Its stupa was dismantled in the nineteenth century, before scholars understood its value.
Why not the others: (A) Sanchi is near Bhopal and (B) Bharhut is in Satna district, both in Madhya Pradesh. (D) Sarnath, where the Buddha gave his first sermon, is near Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh.
Key point: Sanchi survived largely intact, while Amaravati's sculptures were carried off to Calcutta, Madras and London.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: The Mughal Empire and Agrarian Society
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Khud-kashta
(B) Pahi-kashta
(C) Muqaddam
(D) Jins-i kamil

List-II (Meaning)
(I) Non-resident cultivators who belonged to another village
(II) Perfect crops, such as cotton and sugarcane, that earned more revenue
(III) Headman of the village panchayat
(IV) Peasants who lived in the village in which they held land
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Why: Khud-kashta peasants lived in the village where they held land (IV). Pahi-kashta cultivators came from other villages, sometimes because of better terms (I). The muqaddam or mandal headed the panchayat (III). Jins-i kamil were the "perfect crops" (II).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the two kinds of peasants. (C) swaps the pahi-kashta and the headman. (D) swaps the headman and the perfect crops.
Key point: The Mughal state encouraged jins-i kamil crops because they brought in more revenue.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part III: Revolt of 1857: Patterns and Representations
questions.question: In 1851, ____ described the kingdom of Awadh as "a cherry that will drop into our mouth one day". Five years later the kingdom was annexed.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Lord Dalhousie
Why: Governor-General Lord Dalhousie used these words in 1851. Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the grounds of misgovernment.
Why not the others: (A) Wellesley imposed the subsidiary alliance on Awadh in 1801. (C) Canning succeeded Dalhousie. (D) Cornwallis belongs to the 1790s.
Key point: The annexation displaced Nawab Wajid Ali Shah and the taluqdars, so Awadh became a centre of the revolt.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Social Histories of Early Societies: Mahabharata
questions.question: In the study of kinship and marriage, the practice of marrying within a unit, such as a kin group, caste or a group living in the same locality, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Endogamy
Why: Endogamy means marriage within a unit.
Why not the others: (A) Exogamy is marriage outside a unit, as with the gotra rule. (C) Polygyny is a man having several wives. (D) Polyandry is a woman having several husbands, as in Draupadi's marriage to the Pandavas.
Key point: The gotra rule made marriage exogamous with respect to the gotra.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part II: Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Traveller)
(A) Al-Biruni
(B) Ibn Battuta
(C) François Bernier
(D) Abdur Razzaq Samarqandi

List-II (Work or role)
(I) *Rihla*, a travel account written in Arabic
(II) Ambassador from Herat who visited south India and Vijayanagara in the 1440s
(III) *Kitab-ul-Hind*, a work in Arabic on Indian society and religion
(IV) *Travels in the Mughal Empire*, which compared India with Europe
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Al-Biruni wrote the *Kitab-ul-Hind* (III). Ibn Battuta's account is the *Rihla* (I). Bernier wrote *Travels in the Mughal Empire* (IV). Abdur Razzaq Samarqandi came as an ambassador from Herat in the 1440s (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two works. (B) swaps Bernier and Abdur Razzaq. (D) gives Bernier's book to al-Biruni.
Key point: Al-Biruni (eleventh century), Ibn Battuta (fourteenth) and Bernier (seventeenth) are the three main travellers in NCERT.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Political and Economic Systems in Early States: Inscriptional Evidences
questions.question: The earliest coins of the subcontinent, which came into use from about the sixth century BCE, are called ____ coins and were made mainly of silver and copper.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Punch-marked
Why: Punch-marked coins were made of silver and copper and stamped with symbols. They have been found at many sites across the subcontinent.
Why not the others: (A) Gold coins were first issued on a large scale by the Kushanas, and the Guptas issued some of the most spectacular ones. (B) and (C) are not the names NCERT gives to the earliest coins.
Key point: Punch-marked coins may have been issued by kings, merchants, bankers or townspeople.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.sub_topic: What was laid out first in the Lower Town
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

When excavators cleared the Lower Town of Mohenjodaro, they found that the settlement had been planned before it was built. Streets and lanes were laid out on an approximate grid, crossing at right angles, and the drains were put down first; the houses were then built along them. Every house had to have at least one wall along a street so that its waste water could flow into the street drain.

The street drains were made of bricks set in mortar and were covered with loose bricks that could be lifted for cleaning. Long channels had sumps at intervals where waste collected and could be cleared out. Bathrooms inside houses were paved with bricks and their drains ran through the outer wall. One of the excavators, Ernest Mackay, judged it the most complete ancient system of drainage then known.

The bricks themselves, whether sun-dried or baked, followed a standard ratio: the length was four times the height and the breadth twice the height. Houses had no windows in the walls along the ground level, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard. On the western side stood the Citadel, smaller but higher than the Lower Town, built on mud-brick platforms and walled.

Question: According to the passage, which part of the Lower Town of Mohenjodaro was laid out before the houses were built?
options: A) The Citadel walls around the settlement
B) The brick platforms for every house
C) The street drains along the planned streets
D) The public wells inside the courtyards
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The street drains along the planned streets
Why: The passage says the drains "were put down first; the houses were then built along them". Every house needed one wall on a street so that its waste water reached the street drain.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) describe the Citadel, which stood apart on the west; nothing says house platforms came before drains. (D) wells are not mentioned in the passage.
Key point: Laying drains before houses is NCERT's main evidence that the settlement was planned first and then built.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

When excavators cleared the Lower Town of Mohenjodaro, they found that the settlement had been planned before it was built. Streets and lanes were laid out on an approximate grid, crossing at right angles, and the drains were put down first; the houses were then built along them. One of the excavators, Ernest Mackay, judged it the most complete ancient system of drainage then known.

The bricks themselves, whether sun-dried or baked, followed a standard ratio: the length was four times the height and the breadth twice the height. Houses had no windows in the walls along the ground level, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard. On the western side stood the Citadel, smaller but higher than the Lower Town, built on mud-brick platforms and walled.

Question: Following the passage, what was the ratio of length, breadth and height in Harappan bricks?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4 : 2 : 1
Why: The length was four times the height and the breadth twice the height, so length : breadth : height = 4 : 2 : 1.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) do not fit "four times" and "twice" the height.
Key point: The same brick ratio was used across Harappan sites, which suggests a common standard for the whole region.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.sub_topic: Features of the Citadel at Mohenjodaro
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

When excavators cleared the Lower Town of Mohenjodaro, they found that the settlement had been planned before it was built. Streets and lanes were laid out on an approximate grid, crossing at right angles, and the drains were put down first; the houses were then built along them. Long channels had sumps at intervals where waste collected and could be cleared out. Bathrooms inside houses were paved with bricks and their drains ran through the outer wall. One of the excavators, Ernest Mackay, judged it the most complete ancient system of drainage then known.

The bricks themselves, whether sun-dried or baked, followed a standard ratio: the length was four times the height and the breadth twice the height. Houses had no windows in the walls along the ground level, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard. On the western side stood the Citadel, smaller but higher than the Lower Town, built on mud-brick platforms and walled.

Question: Which description of the Citadel at Mohenjodaro is supported by the passage?
options: A) It lay on the eastern side and was larger but lower than the Lower Town
B) It was an unwalled market area spread out around the main street drains
C) It lay to the north and was built of stone blocks without any platforms
D) It lay on the western side and was smaller but higher, on brick platforms
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It lay on the western side and was smaller but higher, on brick platforms
Why: The passage says the Citadel stood "on the western side", was "smaller but higher than the Lower Town", was built on mud-brick platforms and was walled.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the direction and the size. (B) contradicts the walling. (C) gets the direction and the building material wrong.
Key point: The Citadel's height came from its mud-brick platforms. Structures such as the Great Bath and the warehouse stood there.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

When excavators cleared the Lower Town of Mohenjodaro, they found that the settlement had been planned before it was built. One of the excavators, Ernest Mackay, judged it the most complete ancient system of drainage then known.

The bricks themselves, whether sun-dried or baked, followed a standard ratio: the length was four times the height and the breadth twice the height. Houses had no windows in the walls along the ground level, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard. On the western side stood the Citadel, smaller but higher than the Lower Town, built on mud-brick platforms and walled.

Question: What does the passage suggest about the design of houses in the Lower Town?
options: A) Large windows faced the street so that traders could display goods
B) The design shielded the inside of the house from people on the street
C) Each house opened directly into a public bath at the back
D) Houses were built without bathrooms and used shared drains only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The design shielded the inside of the house from people on the street
Why: There were no windows in the walls along the ground level, and the entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard. NCERT reads this as a concern for privacy.
Why not the others: (A) contradicts the absence of ground-level windows. (C) is not in the passage. (D) contradicts the paved bathrooms whose drains ran through the outer wall.
Key point: The courtyard was the centre of the house, used for cooking and weaving in hot and dry weather.

questions.topic: Themes in Indian History Part I: Harappan Civilisation and Archaeology
questions.question:
Read the following source passage and answer the question that follows.

When excavators cleared the Lower Town of Mohenjodaro, they found that the settlement had been planned before it was built. Streets and lanes were laid out on an approximate grid, crossing at right angles, and the drains were put down first; the houses were then built along them. The street drains were made of bricks set in mortar and were covered with loose bricks that could be lifted for cleaning. Long channels had sumps at intervals where waste collected and could be cleared out. Bathrooms inside houses were paved with bricks and their drains ran through the outer wall. One of the excavators, Ernest Mackay, judged it the most complete ancient system of drainage then known.

The bricks themselves, whether sun-dried or baked, followed a standard ratio: the length was four times the height and the breadth twice the height. Houses had no windows in the walls along the ground level, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard. On the western side stood the Citadel, smaller but higher than the Lower Town, built on mud-brick platforms and walled.

Question: Which conclusion follows most directly from the description of drains in the passage?
options: A) Each household dug and maintained its own drain without any common rule
B) Drains were added only after the city became crowded and unhealthy
C) Some authority planned the layout and enforced rules such as street-facing walls
D) The drainage system was copied from Mesopotamian cities after trade began
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Some authority planned the layout and enforced rules such as street-facing walls
Why: The drains were laid before the houses, every house had to join a street drain, and long channels had sumps for cleaning. All of this needs planning and a rule followed by everyone, which points to an authority able to plan and carry it out.
Why not the others: (A) ignores the common layout and the rule about street walls. (B) contradicts "the drains were put down first". (D) has no basis in the passage.
Key point: Standard bricks, planned drains and the grid layout are NCERT's evidence for complex decisions being made and implemented.
